question: Move the AED at DREAM Charter Elementary and Middle School into a 24/7 outdoor cabinet on the building's street wall.

evidence.text: DREAM Charter Elementary and Middle School (School, ZIP 10029) has a registered AED at "Third Floor; Main Entrance/Lobby".
Its hours come from: School building assumed open 7 AM to 6 PM on school days, September to June. Move the school-hours control to test other closing times.
Under that assumption it is reachable 55 of 168 hours in a school-year week, and 0 hours in a summer week if it is a school.
In 2025, an expected 1.18 cardiac-arrest 911 calls a year came from inside its two-minute walking area at hours when every AED in reach was shut (rank 8 of 100 NYC schools).
Within 400 m there are 11 other registered AED locations; 0 of them are open 24/7 by their published hours.
Citywide, a time-blind map puts 4.6% of call-weighted area within a two-minute walk of an AED; at the hour calls actually came in, 1.4% was within reach of one confirmed open.
Published research: a bystander shock with a public AED was associated with survival to discharge of 66.5% versus 43.0% without (Pollack et al., Circulation 2018, observed shockable public arrests).
Overture Maps lists The Mount Sinai Hospital, a hospital normally staffed around the clock, 184 m away: a possible alternative host for a 24/7 AED.
Unknown to this data: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, whether the school already allows after-hours access, and the actual location of each 2025 call inside the ZIP (only ZIP-level data is public).

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: Moving DREAM Charter's AED to a 24/7 outdoor cabinet addresses a real gap in emergency access. The school's current location is reachable only 55 of 168 hours during the school year [E2], leaving the neighborhood without nearby AED coverage during nights, weekends, and summer. Last year, an expected 1.18 cardiac arrests occurred in the surrounding two-minute walking area when every nearby AED was closed [E4]. Research shows bystander defibrillation improves survival to discharge from 43.0% to 66.5% [E7]. While Mount Sinai Hospital sits 184 meters away [E8], a street-accessible cabinet would ensure immediate availability during the critical first minutes of cardiac arrest.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The advocate overstates what we know. Yes, the current AED is inaccessible 113 of 168 school-year hours [E3], but we don't know if those closures actually caused the 1.18 expected annual calls [E4]—the data only shows ZIP code, not whether victims were even near DREAM Charter [E9]. The 66.5% survival figure [E7] comes from shockable arrests where bystanders were already present; it doesn't tell us how many cardiac arrests in this neighborhood would actually benefit from a street cabinet versus reaching Mount Sinai 184 meters away [E8]. Before committing resources, we need cabinet costs, vandalism risk, and whether those 1.18 calls cluster at times a cabinet would help [E9]. Eleven other AEDs exist nearby [E5]—better to understand why none are 24/7 first.

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: The skeptic is right that we lack ZIP-level detail on where the 1.18 calls actually occurred [E9], so we cannot prove they happened near DREAM Charter specifically. However, the neighborhood-wide data still supports action. Citywide, only 1.4% of call-weighted area reaches an open AED at the hour calls come in, versus 4.6% on a time-blind map [E6]—a gap that suggests timing, not just location, drives access failures. DREAM Charter's current 55-of-168-hour availability [E2] falls well below that citywide baseline. A 24/7 cabinet removes timing as a barrier for any cardiac arrest in the two-minute zone, regardless of exact address. The skeptic's point about Mount Sinai [E8] is fair, but 184 meters is not guaranteed faster than a street cabinet during the critical first minutes when bystanders act. Without cabinet costs or vandalism data [E9], we cannot rule out the proposal as impractical.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The advocate is right that timing matters citywide [E6], but that doesn't mean DREAM Charter's cabinet solves it here. We still don't know whether the 1.18 expected annual calls [E4] happened when a street cabinet would help, or whether they clustered in summer when the school closes entirely [E3]. The advocate assumes bystanders will find and use an outdoor cabinet faster than reaching Mount Sinai 184 meters away [E8], but that's untested locally. Before we invest in a cabinet, we need to know its cost, vandalism risk [E9], and why the eleven nearby AEDs aren't 24/7 already [E5]—those barriers may apply here too. The survival data [E7] is real, but it doesn't tell us how many neighborhood arrests would actually benefit from this specific location versus alternatives.

verdict.summary: Strong case for access gap (1.18 annual calls during AED closure [E4], citywide timing problem [E6], survival benefit [E7]), but critical unknowns block decision: actual call locations within ZIP [E9], cabinet costs, vandalism risk, and why 11 nearby AEDs remain closed [E5].
verdict.strongestFor: Expected 1.18 cardiac arrests yearly occur when all nearby AEDs closed [E4]; bystander shock improves survival 43.0% to 66.5% [E7].
verdict.strongestAgainst: Call locations unknown within ZIP [E9]; 11 other AEDs nearby all closed [E5]; Mount Sinai 184 m away [E8]; cabinet cost and vandalism risk unknown [E9].
verdict.nextStep: Map 2025 cardiac-arrest call locations within two-minute radius; assess cabinet cost, vandalism history at similar sites, and barriers preventing 24/7 operation at nearby AEDs [E5].
